mcqs.question: How does GPU shared memory differ from a CPU cache?
options: Shared memory is automatically populated by hardware, exactly like a CPU cache
Shared memory is explicitly managed by the programmer — data must be deliberately written into it before threads in the block can reuse it
Shared memory is slower than global memory but larger in capacity
Shared memory is visible to every thread on the entire GPU, not just one block
mcqs.explanation: Shared memory requires explicit writes by the kernel; it isn't transparently filled the way a hardware cache is. It's faster (not slower) than global memory, smaller in capacity, and scoped to a thread block, not the whole GPU.

mcqs.question: Why does the GPU memory hierarchy mirror the thread/block/grid execution hierarchy?
options: It's an arbitrary naming convention with no functional relationship to execution scope
Because memory scope is designed to match cooperation boundaries — threads in the same block share fast memory, while unrelated blocks only meet in the slow global pool
Because registers are actually shared across the entire grid, not just one thread
Because global memory is only accessible to a single thread block at a time
mcqs.explanation: The memory scopes are deliberately aligned to execution scopes so cooperating threads (same block) get a fast shared channel. Registers are strictly per-thread, and global memory is accessible grid-wide, not restricted to one block.

mcqs.question: What does memory coalescing do?
options: It compresses data in global memory to save capacity
It merges the memory requests of threads in a warp accessing adjacent addresses into one wide transaction
It automatically moves frequently-used global data into shared memory
It reorders instructions within a warp to reduce branch divergence
mcqs.explanation: Coalescing is specifically about merging adjacent-address requests from a warp into a single wide memory transaction. It doesn't compress data, doesn't auto-populate shared memory, and has nothing to do with branch divergence.

mcqs.question: A kernel accesses a matrix column-wise while it's stored row-major in global memory. What's the most likely performance impact?
options: None — the GPU compiler automatically transposes the data layout to fix this
Coalescing breaks because threads in a warp now hit scattered, non-adjacent addresses, turning one wide transaction into many small ones
The kernel will fail to compile because column-wise access is not supported
Performance improves because column access reduces bank conflicts in global memory
mcqs.explanation: Mismatched access patterns against memory layout defeat coalescing, often costing an order of magnitude in effective bandwidth. Compilers don't silently re-layout data, the kernel compiles fine, and this access pattern hurts rather than helps throughput.
